questions.question: Which optimizer and learning rate were used to pre-train the BERT model?

statements.text: The BERT model is pre-trained using Adam with a learning rate of 1e-4.

questions.question: Does making the network bigger help accuracy on the GLUE benchmark?

statements.text: Larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets evaluated in the model size study.

citations.quote: We can see that larger models lead to a strict accuracy improvement across all four datasets, even for MRPC which only has 3,600 labeled training examples, and is substantially different from the pre-training tasks.

statements.text: Scaling to extreme model sizes leads to large improvements on very small-scale tasks when the model has been sufficiently pre-trained.

citations.quote: However, we believe that this is the first work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided that the model has been sufficiently pre-trained.

statements.text: For original positive effects reported as numerical values, the median effect size for replications was 85% smaller than the median of the original effect sizes.

statements.text: Overall, 92% of replication effect sizes were smaller than the original findings.

citations.quote: Combining these results, the effect sizes in the replications were smaller than the effect sizes in the original findings in 108 of 118 (92%) cases.

statements.text: When comparing animal and non-animal experiments, median effect sizes were 84% smaller than original findings for animal replications and 78% smaller for non-animal replications.

questions.question: Did studies in living animals reproduce as well as studies without animals?

statements.text: Descriptively, animal experiments with positive effects were less likely to replicate than non-animal experiments with positive effects on every replication criterion.

citations.quote: Descriptively, animal experiments with positive effects were less likely to replicate than non-animal experiments with positive effects on every replication criterion.

statements.text: Animal experiments had lower replication rates, particularly according to the statistical significance criterion, because their original effect sizes were notably smaller than those in original non-animal experiments.

citations.quote: The reason that animal experiments had such a low replication rate, particularly according to the statistical significance criterion (12%), is that the effect sizes in the original experiments (Mdn = 1.61) were notably smaller than the effect sizes in the original non-animal experiments (Mdn = 3.65; Figure 5).

statements.text: However, a multi-level analysis does not support the conclusion that there is a meaningful difference in the replication rates of animal and non-animal experiments.

statements.text: When seeking to predict a successful replication, knowing the original effect size is more useful than knowing whether the experiment involved animals.

citations.quote: In other words, when seeking to predict if a replication will be successful it is more useful to know the original effect size than to know whether the original experiment was an animal experiment or not.

questions.question: Why are results from underpowered, small studies less trustworthy?

statements.text: Because smaller studies in a scientific field mean less likely research findings are to be true, findings from underpowered, early-phase clinical trials are true about one in four times or even less frequently if bias is present.

citations.quote: Corollary 1: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientifi c fi eld, the less likely the research fi ndings are to be true.
